Noise Reduction and Overfitting Prevention for Sebuleni Pro Max AI

This note translates the project architecture into concrete protection rules against noisy learning and false generalization. It incorporates the clarification that the model learns from the full training period while validation and test remain isolated, and it now reflects the exact operating context: single-instrument training from 1-minute OHLC data with higher timeframes created by resampling.

Training split clarification

Your clarification is the correct one for this kind of system. The model should learn from all samples inside the designated training period, not from a subset of training data labeled “unseen.” The truly unseen portions are the validation and test ranges, which must remain untouched by optimization, threshold fitting, regime tuning, calibration fitting, and explanation index construction until their designated evaluation stage.

In practical terms, the split logic should be: training data is fully visible to fitting, validation data is used only to choose architecture and stopping behavior, and test data is reserved for final unbiased assessment. For a time-series system, this chronological separation matters more than the ordinary machine-learning idea of random holdout, because any leakage from future windows will make the model appear more intelligent than it really is.

Core rule

The model may learn from the entire training horizon. It must never learn from validation or test, directly or indirectly, through normalization statistics, event threshold tuning, calibration, regime definitions, or analogy retrieval indexes.

Where noise enters this model

This architecture has more than one noise source. Some noise comes from raw OHLC bars, some from the self-supervised price-move label construction, some from the resampling and multi-timeframe fusion logic, and some from the adaptive regime machinery. If these are not separated conceptually, the team can easily apply the wrong fix to the wrong failure mode.

Raw signal noise

Bad bars, gaps, timestamp errors, duplicate candles, and resampling defects can distort the state learned by the backbone.

Label noise

Self-supervised event labels can be wrong if price-difference thresholds mark chaotic micro-moves as true precursors of meaningful price expansion.

Fusion noise

Bad alignment between 1m, 15m, 1h, 4h, and 1d windows can create false cross-timeframe relationships.

Adaptation noise

Online updates and regime creation can overreact to temporary disturbances and turn noise into false structural change.

Noise prevention measures

Data-level controls

The first defense should happen before the data reaches the model. The 1-minute OHLC source needs strict timestamp validation, duplicate removal, candle continuity checks, gap flags, and bar-integrity sanity checks. Do not silently repair everything. Missingness, suspicious spikes, and stale intervals should often become explicit model inputs or confidence penalties rather than hidden preprocessing decisions.

For scale-sensitive price features, robust normalization is better than fragile standardization. Use statistics fitted on the training range only, and prefer transforms that are resistant to outliers, such as median and interquartile based scaling, clipped return transforms where appropriate, or winsorization of extreme anomalies that are clearly data defects rather than genuine price events.

Event-label controls

The self-supervised label builder is one of the highest-risk noise points in the whole project. If the price-difference threshold is too low, the model will learn market chatter instead of meaningful precursor states. If the horizon is too wide, the positive class becomes temporally vague and the model will confuse distant possibility with imminent formation. The label construction process therefore needs hysteresis and separation rules.

Use a minimum price-move magnitude, a minimum persistence requirement, and a cool-down interval between nearby events so that a single turbulent period is not counted as many separate positives. Positive windows should end before the event begins, while ambiguous windows near incomplete or overlapping events should be excluded rather than forced into positive or negative classes.

Multi-timeframe controls

The multi-timeframe architecture only helps if resampling and alignment are trustworthy. Each higher timeframe must be built correctly from the 1-minute OHLC stream, and each lower-frame window must be attached to the correct parent bars without ever borrowing future parent context. When a parent bar is incomplete, either use only information available up to the current timestamp or mark that higher-frame state as provisional. Otherwise the lower-frame encoder will accidentally train on future directional context.

Use separate per-timeframe encoders first, and do not let cross-timeframe attention dominate too early. This keeps the model from latching onto noisy short-term correlations before each timeframe has learned its own internal structure.

Regime and MoE controls

The regime detector and the mixture-of-experts router can amplify noise if they are too reactive. A temporary error burst should not instantly become a new regime. Require persistence, multi-metric confirmation, and preferably cross-timeframe agreement before declaring structural change. That means latent drift, error drift, and duration should all point in the same direction before the system commits.

For the experts themselves, prevent expert collapse by encouraging balanced routing and by setting a minimum evidence threshold before a specialist becomes active. A new expert should be born only when the current routing repeatedly fails and the failure persists beyond a short-lived disturbance.

Inference-time noise suppression

The model should not react to one noisy candle or short burst the same way it reacts to a forming event. Smooth the final event probability, drift score, and timing outputs over a short causal window. This smoothing should happen at the decision layer, not by rewriting the raw OHLC history. That way the system remains responsive while still avoiding jumpy outputs that are caused by one-off noise.

Overfitting prevention measures

Split discipline and leakage prevention

The strongest anti-overfitting measure in this project is strict temporal separation. Fit scalers, imputers, regime clusters, confidence calibrators, and FAISS indexes only on training data. Validation should be used for early stopping, hyperparameter choice, and confidence calibration selection if you intentionally split calibration from training. Test must remain frozen until the end.

A common hidden failure in time-series systems is indirect leakage through engineered features. Any rolling mean, rolling quantile, normalization window, candle-derived statistic, or higher-timeframe aggregation must be computed using only information available up to that timestamp. This rule is especially important here because the 15-minute, 1-hour, 4-hour, and 1-day views are all resampled from the same 1-minute base stream.

Architecture-level regularization

The backbone should be strong enough to learn real OHLC temporal structure, but not so large that it memorizes quirks of the training period. Start with moderate embedding sizes, limited attention depth, dropout in both encoder and heads, weight decay, and sparse expert usage. For the prediction heads, keep them narrow. Their job is to read the learned state, not to become separate memorization engines.

For multi-task learning, balance losses carefully. If one head dominates the gradient flow, the backbone starts over-specializing to that task and the other heads become passengers. Use task-weight tuning and monitor whether event performance improves while boundary or timing generalization quietly degrades.

Training schedule controls

The progressive schedule you already outlined is a good anti-overfitting mechanism if applied strictly. First train each timeframe encoder on its own forecasting task. Then add cross-timeframe attention with the base encoders partly frozen. Then unfreeze gradually for joint optimization. This prevents the full stack from co-adapting too quickly around spurious correlations.

Use early stopping on validation metrics that reflect the real objective, not only raw reconstruction loss. For this project, that means watching event F1, calibration quality, boundary coverage, timing error, and regime false alarm rate together. A model that keeps reducing training loss while worsening calibration or false-alarm behavior is already overfitting.

Class balance and hard-negative design

Large events are usually rarer than ordinary motion, which creates a natural imbalance problem. If not handled well, the model will overfit either by becoming too conservative or by memorizing the positive set. Use balanced sampling, focal loss or class-weighted loss where justified, and carefully chosen hard negatives that look similar to precursors but do not lead to the event. This teaches discrimination rather than memorization.

Calibration and explanation safeguards

Overfitting is not only about point accuracy. A model can overfit and still look numerically good while being badly miscalibrated. That is especially dangerous here because the system expresses confidence. Use post-training calibration on validation-only outputs and track expected calibration error, Brier score, interval coverage, and reliability drift over time.

The explanation engine also needs protection. Do not build the analogy index from validation or test embeddings. During evaluation, retrieve analogs only from the training memory bank. Otherwise the explanation subsystem will leak future evidence into the forecast story.

Risk area Failure mode Prevention measure What to monitor
Raw data Defective spikes and irregular timestamps distort latent states Gap flags, duplicate checks, robust scaling, defect clipping, causal imputations Missingness rate, spike rate, per-timeframe continuity
Self-supervised labels Threshold logic turns noise into positives Persistence rules, cool-down windows, ambiguous-zone exclusion, minimum event separation Positive rate stability, label overlap, event purity review
Multi-timeframe fusion Future-aware parent context leaks downward Strict timestamp alignment, provisional parent bars, causal feature generation only Alignment audits, leakage tests, ablation results
MoE routing Experts memorize slices of training data or collapse to one expert Routing regularization, minimum support thresholds, delayed expert birth, load balancing Expert usage entropy, per-expert validation gap
Online learning Short-term disturbance triggers false adaptation Persistence thresholds, rollback checkpoints, shadow evaluation before promotion Error bursts, drift persistence, rollback frequency
Confidence layer Overconfident predictions hide overfitting Validation-only calibration, interval coverage checks, reliability monitoring ECE, Brier score, PICP, interval width
Explanation engine Future examples contaminate historical analogs Training-only retrieval bank during evaluation Retrieval provenance, time-consistency audits

Recommended operating rules

  1. Use the full training horizon for fitting, but fit every preprocessing statistic only on training data.
  2. Build self-supervised labels with persistence rules and event separation so the model learns meaningful precursors, not turbulence.
  3. Train timeframe encoders independently before enabling cross-timeframe attention.
  4. Require persistent evidence before declaring a new regime or creating a new expert.
  5. Keep the heads smaller than the shared backbone so the system learns general state first and task specifics second.
  6. Use validation to stop training and calibrate trust, not to fit the model.
  7. Evaluate explanations against a training-only memory bank to prevent analog leakage.
  8. Promote online updates only after they outperform the current model on a protected recent validation slice.
  9. Track calibration and false alarm rate with the same seriousness as directional accuracy.
  10. If noise rises sharply, widen uncertainty and reduce confidence before changing the regime structure.
Best single design principle

Do not let the system treat every unusual pattern as new information. First ask whether it is defective data, transient disturbance, unresolved ambiguity, or genuine structural change. Each of those requires a different response.

Final advice

For this project, noise reduction and overfitting prevention are not separate tasks. They are both about protecting the shared latent state from learning the wrong story. If noisy labels, bad alignment, future leakage, or over-reactive regime logic corrupt that state, every downstream head will inherit the mistake.

The strongest version of this platform will be one that is conservative in what it treats as structure, disciplined about temporal separation, and honest about uncertainty when the signal is weak. That is how you keep an adaptive system intelligent without letting it become unstable or self-deceptive.
